3.1.crux: Synthetic fibres are made by people from chemicals; each fibre is a polymer, a long chain of small repeating units.

cards.title: Natural or synthetic?
say: The clothes we wear are made of fibres.
Fibres made by people are called synthetic or man-made fibres.

cards.title: A chain of small units

labels.name: Link
labels.note: Units are joined to each other

say: A synthetic fibre is a very long chain of small units joined together.
Such a large unit made of many small units is called a polymer.
cards.remember: 'Poly' means many and 'mer' means part: a polymer is many parts joined.

cards.title: Like paper clips
say: Join many paper clips end to end and you get a long chain.
A polymer is built the same way from tiny units.

cards.title: Natural polymers too
say: Polymers occur in nature too: cotton is made of cellulose, a natural polymer.
Most synthetic fibres are made from chemicals obtained from petroleum.

crux_points: Synthetic fibres are made by people, natural fibres come from plants and animals.
A polymer is a long chain of small repeating units.
Most synthetic fibres are made from petrochemicals.

options: A long chain of small repeating units
quiz.why: Polymers are made by joining many small units into a long chain.

quiz.q: Which of these is a synthetic fibre?
quiz.why: Nylon is made in factories; cotton, wool and jute are natural.

3.2.crux: The main synthetic fibres are rayon, nylon, polyester and acrylic; each is used where its special property helps.

cards.title: Four synthetic fibres

items.name: Rayon
items.eg: From wood pulp; looks like silk

say: Each fibre is made differently and has its own special features.

cards.title: Rayon: artificial silk

steps.text: Wood pulp is treated with chemicals
A shiny fibre, rayon, is made
Mixed with cotton for bed sheets, or with wool for carpets

say: Rayon looks like silk but is much cheaper.
It is called artificial silk.

cards.title: Nylon: stronger than steel wire
say: Nylon, made in 1931, was the first fully synthetic fibre.
A nylon thread is stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness. It is also light, elastic and easy to wash.

cards.title: Polyester and acrylic

cols.head: Polyester
cells: Shirts, sarees; PET bottles and films

say: Terylene is a popular polyester. Mixed with cotton it becomes 'terrycot'.
PET, a kind of polyester, is used to make bottles and containers.

crux_points: Rayon is made from wood pulp and looks like silk.
Nylon is very strong and elastic: ropes, parachutes, tents.
Polyester stays crease-free; acrylic is a cheap substitute for wool.

quiz.why: Rayon is made from wood pulp and looks like silk.

quiz.q: Which fibre would you choose for a climbing rope?
quiz.why: Nylon is very strong and elastic, so it is used for climbing ropes and parachutes.

quiz.q: Sweaters that look like wool but cost less are usually made of…
quiz.why: Acrylic looks and feels like wool but is cheaper.

3.3.crux: Synthetic fibres are popular because they are strong, last long, dry quickly and cost less, but they melt when heated.

cards.title: Why people like them
say: Synthetic fibres absorb less water, so they dry quickly.
They last a long time and are cheaper than natural fibres.

cards.title: The big danger: melting

cols.head: Cotton clothes near fire
cells: Best in the kitchen and lab

say: If synthetic clothes catch fire, the melted fibre sticks to the skin.
So we should never wear synthetic clothes while cooking or working in a laboratory.
cards.remember: Wear cotton, not synthetics, near a stove or flame.

cards.title: Wet test

cols.head: Cotton or wool cloth
cells: Soaks up a lot of water

say: Soak the same size of different cloths and see which dries first.
Synthetic cloth soaks up less water, so it dries faster.

crux_points: Synthetic fibres are strong, durable, cheap and easy to care for.
They absorb little water, so they dry quickly.
They melt on heating, so they are dangerous near fire.

quiz.q: Why should you not wear synthetic clothes while cooking?
options: They melt and stick to the skin if they catch fire
quiz.why: Synthetic fibres melt on heating and can cause severe burns.

quiz.q: Why does a nylon cloth dry faster than a cotton one?
quiz.why: Synthetic fibres hold less water, so they dry quickly.

3.4.crux: Plastics are polymers too: thermoplastics soften again on heating, but thermosetting plastics stay hard once moulded.

cards.title: Two kinds of plastic

cols.head: Thermosetting
cells: No, it stays hard once set

say: Plastic can be moulded into any shape.
Some plastics bend on heating; others don't.
cards.remember: Thermo-PLASTIC can be reshaped; thermo-SETTING is set for good.

cards.title: Bakelite and melamine

items.name: Bakelite
items.eg: Poor conductor of heat and electricity: switches, pan handles

items.name: Melamine
items.eg: Resists fire and heat: kitchenware, floor tiles, fire-proof fabrics

say: Bakelite is used in electrical switches because it does not conduct electricity.
Melamine is used to make crockery and fabric that resists fire.

cards.title: Chains: straight or linked

cols.head: Long straight chains
cells: Chains slide past each other when warm

cols.head: Chains linked across
cells: Chains are locked in a net

say: In some plastics the chains are straight; in others they are cross-linked like a net.
Cross-linked chains can't move, so the plastic stays hard.

crux_points: Plastics are polymers that can be moulded into shapes.
Thermoplastics (polythene, PVC) soften and reshape on heating.
Thermosetting plastics (bakelite, melamine) stay hard once moulded.

quiz.why: Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic that does not conduct electricity or heat.

quiz.q: A plastic bottle bends when you put it in hot water. It is a…
quiz.why: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be reshaped.

3.5.crux: Plastics are used everywhere because they don't rust, are light, strong, last long and don't conduct heat or electricity.

cards.title: Why we choose plastic

items.sub: Easy to make in any shape

say: Water and air do not react with plastic, so it doesn't rust like iron.

cards.title: Plastics in hospitals and homes
say: Teflon is a special plastic that oil and water don't stick to.
Many medical items are plastic because they can be thrown away after one use.

cards.title: In planes and cars
say: Plastics replace heavy metal parts in cars, planes and trains.

crux_points: Plastics don't rust or react with most substances.
They are light, strong, durable and cheap.
They don't conduct heat or electricity, so they are used for handles and wire covers.

quiz.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic?
quiz.why: Plastic is a poor conductor of electricity, so it keeps us safe.

quiz.q: What is used to make non-stick cookware?
quiz.why: Teflon is a plastic coating that food, oil and water don't stick to.

3.6.crux: Plastics don't rot away (they are non-biodegradable), so they pile up and harm animals and the land; we must follow the 4 Rs.

cards.title: How long things take to break down

steps.text: Vegetable and fruit peels: 1 to 2 weeks
Tin and aluminium cans: 100 to 500 years

say: Things that rot naturally because of bacteria are biodegradable.
Plastic is non-biodegradable: it stays in the soil for years.

cards.title: Harm done by plastic
say: Plastic thrown away carelessly ends up in drains, fields and animals' stomachs.
Burning plastic is not a solution: it releases poisonous fumes.

cards.title: The 4 Rs

steps.text: Use less plastic; carry a cloth or jute bag.
Use containers again instead of throwing them away.
Send plastics to be melted and made into new things.
Get useful energy or material back from waste.

say: Separate waste: biodegradable in one bin, plastics and cans in another.

crux_points: Biodegradable materials rot naturally; plastic does not.
Plastic waste harms animals, blocks drains and pollutes soil; burning it releases poison.
Follow the 4 Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover.

quiz.why: Bacteria cannot break plastic down, so it stays in the environment for years.

quiz.q: Carrying a cloth bag to the market is an example of…
quiz.why: Using a cloth bag reduces the number of plastic bags used.
